data.title: Is it curtains for COLA? Saving Social Security could mean changing the cost-of-living adjustment.
data.description:
By Alessandra Malito

Several proposals consider changing the way retirees receive inflation protection. Here's what it could cost you.

Many Americans rely on the cost-of-living adjustment, but altering it might be one provision in a package to fix the program's insolvency issue.

For U.S. workers, Social Security is a cherished benefit. It's guaranteed lifetime income that adjusts every year to keep up with inflation.

That yearly cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is crucial because it allows older Americans to retain their purchasing power. But with Social Security facing insolvency in the next six years, the way in which recipients receive that perk may change substantially.

The COLA will be 3.6% in 2027, up from 2.8% this year. For the average beneficiary, that means an additional $75 a month. The Social Security Administration uses a formula that's tied to a subset of the Consumer Price Index to calculate the cost of living change each year. While the amount of the increase doesn't always align with what retirees spend, it is a help to those who rely on Social Security to pay the bills.

"People who receive Social Security benefits rely on [the COLA] heavily to protect their buying power," said Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare analyst who has been tracking benefit adjustments for almost 30 years. "It is one of the only forms of retirement income we have that offers inflation adjustment." There are insurance products that offer inflation protection, such as annuities, but retirees have to pay for the perk, she said.

There isn't enough money going into Social Security's trust funds to sustain the program, and experts expect the funds to be depleted in the next six years. If that happens, all beneficiaries could see a cut to benefits of about 26%, and without any legislative changes, those cuts would deepen as the years go on. Congress has not yet seriously deliberated on ways to fix this insolvency issue, but policymakers and experts have floated ideas about eliminating the income-tax cap, raising the Full Retirement Age or finding other ways in which workers and retirees alike can be taxed.

Another possibility: Alter the cost-of-living adjustment.

Revamping the system

One avenue is to incorporate a flat-rate COLA. In a 1987 proposal from former Rep. Tim Penny, a Democrat who represented Minnesota from 1983-1995, the flat-rate strategy would use a benchmark determined by the dollar amount the beneficiary in the 20th percentile received. Put another way, if all Social Security recipients were to be arranged by the amount of their benefit, this strategy would take the bottom 20% and set the rate to the highest benefit in that quintile, leaving 80% of beneficiaries with a smaller adjustment, said Rich Johnson, vice president of financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute.

Johnson used the 2026 COLA as an example. In 2026, beneficiaries received a 2.8% hike to benefits. The actual monthly COLA for the average beneficiary in January 2026 was $58, but if the program used the flat-rate method instead, the adjustment would have only been $34. Comparatively, it would cover a 1.7% inflation rate, he said.

Using this type of flat rate structure would significantly decrease the amount that beneficiaries receive over their lifetimes.

"These cuts would continually take place year after year," AARP's Johnson said. "They accumulate over time." If this change happened in 1998, for example, it would have cost the average beneficiary $78,000 over the past 28 years. "That is the power," he said. "That is why the COLA matters."

Older people receiving Social Security would not see as much of an impact as newly retired individuals who have a longer horizon for receiving benefits, Johnson added. Younger Americans wouldn't be affected at first, but their lifetime benefits would weaken under a reduced COLA system.

This change alone wouldn't solve Social Security's financing problems. There will likely have to be a package of provisions to solve the program's insolvency issue. A flat-rate COLA using the 20th-percentile figure and enacted in 2027 would close half of the program's 75-year shortfall, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, using calculations from Urban Institute's Karen Smith. If it were at the 30th percentile, it would close two-fifths of the shortfall.

Capping the COLA

Under a capped COLA system, recipients would still receive an increase every year, but those with the highest benefits would receive a limited amount.

Anyone above a certain income cutoff would have their COLA capped, and anyone below it, would receive the full increase. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget gave an example: If the cap was set at $900 in 2035 and a retiree receiving $50,000 in benefits would have received a $1,000 COLA under the current system, they would receive $900 instead.

If the cap was set at the COLA for retirees in the 75th percentile, thus affecting the highest quarter of beneficiaries, it would close about 10% of Social Security's 75-year shortfall, saving $115 billion over the span of 10 years.

"A COLA cap would generate immediate savings and meaningfully reduce Social Security's funding gap," the CRFB wrote in an analysis on the proposal.

Switching from CPI-W to CPI-E

Right now, the COLA calculation is linked to CPI-W, the consumer price index for urban workers, and not CPI-E, which tracks the spending of adults 62 and older. Some experts and policymakers have proposed switching to CPI-E, arguing that doing so would better align COLA with retirees' actual spending and potentially provide them with a higher benefit.

The cost of healthcare greatly contributes to how much seniors spend every year, but rapidly growing prices also affect the disparity between the CPI-W and CPI-E, Mary Johnson said. Older Americans spend roughly twice as much on healthcare than younger urban workers, she said.

CPI-E historically outpaces CPI-W, but there have been years, such as 2022 and 2023, when gas prices soared, the COLA was higher than it would have been if it were tied to senior spending.

Switching to CPI-E would be more expensive. If the COLA were calculated using CPI-E beginning in December 2028, the adjustments would expand the long-range shortfall by 7%.

Other options

Another switch could be to a chained COLA, which is a more complicated way to calculate annual adjustments. Then-president Barack Obama included this suggestion in his 2014 budget, but it received pushback and was later dropped.

CPI-W measures the same goods and services, no matter what they cost, but a chained COLA accounts for buyers' substitutions. For example, shoppers at the supermarket may pick up chicken instead of beef if it has become too expensive for them.

This strategy could paint a more accurate picture of how consumers make purchases, but it would also limit the increases to COLA, and that would ultimately result in lower payments as well. A chained CPI starting next year would cut $188 billion of spending between 2027 and 2036 and close about 12% of Social Security's 75-year actuarial shortfall, according to the Cato Institute. "Benefits would generally continue to rise to keep pace with inflation, but more slowly than under the current law," according to its analysis.

Other proposals suggest straightforward cuts, such as reducing the COLA by 0.5 or 1 percentage points. With this strategy, the COLA would be calculated as usual before the reduction occurred, and then cut. The more extreme measure, cutting the COLA by one percentage point, would eliminate 44% of the 75-year shortfall if it began in December 2027, the Social Security Administration said.

Maintaining purchasing power

Legislators will have to strike a delicate balance between keeping Social Security's trust funds afloat and not lowering the COLA too severely. The first automatic COLA was introduced in 1975, in an effort to thwart aggressive inflation the country saw in the 1960s and 1970s.

But the relationship many retirees have with Social Security has changed in the decades since, and retirees are relying much more heavily on the program than ever before, said Robert Conzo, a certified financial planner and chief executive officer of financial advisory firm The Wealth Alliance. "They're using Social Security as their primary source of income," he said. "It was never designed for that."

At least approximately 14% of recipients 65 and older rely on Social Security for 90% or more of their family income, according to a 2024 Census Bureau's Center for Economic Studies report.

Protecting the COLA should be a priority for older Americans, Mary Johnson said. "It is better that we are grateful that we even have one because there are certainly efforts to reduce it or eliminate it altogether for some people," Johnson said. "We want to stick together on this and protect this benefit."

-Alessandra Malito

data.title: Wage growth hits 5-year low as American workers find their take-home pay is 'stretched thinner and thinner'
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Worker compensation grows slower than inflation for second straight quarter

Workers' wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the past year ending in September, according to new data.

American workers are being slammed by higher prices, with new data from the Labor Department showing wages rose at the slowest pace in over five years during the third quarter.

Before adjusting for inflation, wages grew at a 3.1% pace over the past year ending in September, the smallest increase since the first quarter of 2021. That's down from the 3.6% growth rate in the same quarter last year.

The data add evidence of the challenges that consumers are facing coping with rising costs.

Wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the past year ending in September.

"Wage growth has fallen short of inflation, and while increased hours worked can provide somewhat of an offset, workers in many industry groups are finding their take-home pay is being stretched thinner and thinner," wrote Richard Moody, chief economist at Regions Financial Corp.

Inflation, as measured by the Fed's favored personal-consumption-expenditure price index, was running at a 3.6% annual rate in September.

Overall, the cost of employing the average worker, which includes wages and benefits, rose 3.4% in the 12 months that ended in September. This measure, known as the employment cost index, has risen at a steady pace for four straight quarters.

Economists think the ECI is the best measure of trends in labor compensation because it includes the public sector, makes adjustments for the mix of jobs and is better for measuring pay changes with industries. But because it only comes out four times a years, another measure -average hourly earnings - is more closely watched.

According to the ECI data, union workers saw a 4.3% annual increase in compensation, while nonunion workers' compensation costs increased 3.3%.

Meanwhile, employers are also paying more for employee perks. Benefit costs rose at a 3.9% year-over-year pace, according to the ECI data. That's up from 3.6% rate in the same three-month period last year.

"The recent strength in benefits likely indicates that employers were looking for somewhat more flexible and less costly ways to reward strong performance," wrote Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon.

Moody said he expected wage growth to pick up in coming quarters as labor productivity growth has been strong even before AI investment is factored into the equation.

But other analysts, like Oliver Allen, senior U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, thinks wage growth will soften along with weak hiring.

Benefit costs, especially health-insurance plans, will accelerate meaningfully next year, Moody said.

"While firms will pass some of that rising cost burden along to their workers, we expect the net effect to be upward pressure on growth in labor-compensation costs over coming quarters," he wrote.

For the Federal Reserve, stable employment costs are welcome, as rising wages are considered a surefire way to put upward pressure on prices.

"ECI, the Fed's preferred measure of wage inflation, reaffirms other wage data that the labor market is not a source of inflationary pressures," wrote Veronica Clark, an economist at Citi.

-Greg Robb

data.title: ICE Closing Review: Canola Finds Traction
data.description:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba-- Intercontinental Exchange canola futures posted gains on Friday, halting a multi-session slide after getting support from comparable oils.

With the threat of renewed fighting in the Middle East, crude oil was up sharply on Friday, with the spillover flowing into

the vegetable oils. That saw canola underpinned by increases in Chicago soybeans and soyoil, as well as Malaysian palm oil and European rapeseed.

Some pressure came from losses in Chicago soymeal.

Despite today's improvement, the January canola contract remained behind most of its major moving averages, weighing on canola values.

Producer deliveries of canola slipped during the week ended Oct. 25 to 445,900 tonnes. The year-to-date of 5.43 million tonnes

was 1.32 million more than a year ago.

Canola exports nudged up on the week at 238,000 tonnes. Cumulative exports nearly topped 1.89 million tonnes, compared to 1.23 million this time last year.

Domestic use was relatively steady at 196,300 tonnes with the running total of almost 2.99 million tonnes slightly ahead of last year.

The Canadian dollar was higher on Friday afternoon, with the loonie at 71.65 U.S. cents, compared to Wednesday's close of 71.51.

There were 55,387 canola contracts traded on Friday, compared to 78,331 on Thursday. Spreading accounted for 26,094 contracts traded.

data.title: From Prison Classroom to National Audience: "Basement People" Screens at San Quentin Film Festival and Digitally Debuts Nationally on Securus Technologies Tablets
data.description:
From Prison Classroom to National Audience: "Basement People" Screens at San Quentin Film Festival and Digitally Debuts Nationally on Securus Technologies Tablets

From Prison Classroom to National Audience: "Basement People" Screens at San Quentin Film Festival and Digitally Debuts Nationally on Securus Technologies Tablets

PR Newswire

PLANO, Texas, Oct. 30, 2026

Directed by Christine Swanson and winner of Best Short Film at the Martha's Vineyard African American Film Festival, Kyale Akeem Williams' Academy Award-eligible film is now available to incarcerated viewers nationwide

PLANO, Texas, Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Basement People, an Academy Award-eligible short film written by incarcerated screenwriter Kyale Akeem Williams and directed by award-winning filmmaker Christine Swanson, screens at the 2026 San Quentin Film Festival. Technology access inside correctional facilities carried the film from a Michigan prison classroom to the festival circuit and secure tablets nationwide, extending education beyond the classroom, sustaining creative collaboration, and building the connection, skills, and sense of purpose essential to rehabilitation.

On October 22, 2026, Securus Technologies, a technology company that equips more than 1,800 correctional agencies with a comprehensive portfolio of connectivity solutions that enhance public safety and optimize facility operations, made Basement People available to incarcerated viewers through the Securus Media Store. Delivered across Securus' network of more than 550,000 secure tablets in corrections facilities nationwide, the release expands access to meaningful content that can spark reflection, reinforce learning, and bring to life where education and creative work can lead in rehabilitation and reentry.

Williams developed the screenplay through a Calvin Prison Initiative screenwriting course at Michigan's Richard A. Handlon Correctional Facility. Recognizing the strength of his work, Calvin University professor Geert Heetebrij connected Williams with Swanson, a fellow Detroiter who went on to direct the film. Through JPay accounts on the Securus platform, Williams stayed connected with Swanson and the project's broader support network, allowing them to continue developing the screenplay during his incarceration and turn classroom learning into sustained creative collaboration.

"When I first read the script, I was struck by its emotional precision, moral ambiguity, and relatable characters," said Swanson, whose directing credits include The Clark Sisters: First Ladies of Gospel and Albany Road. "It did not ask for pity. It asked for understanding. Now, people inside may see their own families reflected in it, and that means a great deal to me."

The film follows Tina, a seven-year-old girl who retreats to her family's basement after a traumatic incident and finds refuge with her uncle Keith, whom the family has dismissed and isolated. Their bond creates safety without judgment and illustrates how empathy and connection can interrupt cycles of neglect and harm.

"I wrote Basement People to explore how vulnerable family members respond to familial violence, emotional abuse, and mental health conditions," said Williams. "I hope this interpersonal complexity will encourage audiences to sympathize with the protagonist without dehumanizing her tough and aggressive family. After all, each family member is a victim in their own way—someone who also deserves love, mercy, and compassion."

After winning Best Short Film at the Martha's Vineyard African American Film Festival, Basement People earned Academy Award eligibility. Its screening at the San Quentin Film Festival, now in its third year and the first film festival established inside a U.S. prison, brings a screenplay developed inside one correctional facility to an audience inside another, proving how education, creative opportunity, and technology access can carry work beyond institutional walls.

"Access to technology while incarcerated gives individuals an opportunity to discover and develop abilities they may never have had the chance to explore," said Jessica Lust, Chief Product Officer, Securus Technologies. "In particular, secure tablets create connectivity to educational tools, mentors, and collaborators that lead to skill building, motivation, and purpose, which can be the foundations of rehabilitation and successful reentry."

"Our responsibility extends beyond providing services. It includes listening to the communities where we operate and supporting the local people and organizations that understand what their communities need to thrive," said Shamia Lodge, Stakeholder Engagement Director, Securus Technologies. "When we pair their insight with resources that expand access and opportunity, we help create conditions in which more individuals can build lasting success."

About Securus Technologies
Securus Technologies, an Aventiv company and the industry leader, equips more than 1,800 correctional agencies with a comprehensive portfolio of technology solutions that enhance public safety and optimize facility operations. Securus helps agencies bring communications, intelligence, mobility, education, monitoring, and operational visibility together in one integrated ecosystem that improves safety, efficiency, and outcomes. Through purpose-built infrastructure, extensive corrections expertise, and continuous investment in innovation, Securus helps agencies modernize how corrections work while supporting successful reentry and stronger communities.

About Basement People
Basement People explores the impact of trauma poverty, and untreated mental illness on children and urban communities. Through Tina, a sensitive young girl, and her uncle Keith, a man isolated by his own struggles, the film reveals how cycles of neglect and violence can be interrupted by empathy and understanding.

Written by Kyale Akeem Williams, an incarcerated writer at Michigan's Richard A. Handlon Correctional Facility through the Calvin Prison Initiative and directed by award-winning filmmaker Christine Swanson, Basement People unites two artists whose shared roots ground the film in authenticity. This collaboration bridges art, justice and community healing while amplifying Detroit's creative legacy.

data.title: Tidal Wave Auto Spa Opens New Conveyor Car Wash in Merritt Island, Florida
data.description:
THOMASTON, GA / ACCESS Newswire / October 30, 2026 / Tidal Wave Auto Spa®, one of the nation's largest conveyor car wash companies, is pleased to announce the grand opening of its newest conveyor car wash in Merritt Island, Florida. Now open at 55 S Banana River Drive, the new Merritt Island car wash marks the company's 33rd location in the Sunshine State and 339th nationwide.

To celebrate the Grand Opening, the Merritt Island location is offering 12 days of free premium car washes from October 28 to November 8. This limited-time promotion lets customers experience the company's premium wash option, Graph-X4® + Super Shammy, at no cost. The Merritt Island location features mat cleaning stations, complimentary tire air, spot-free rinse, undercarriage wash, foam and wax treatments, and tire shine - delivering a complete car care experience from start to finish. Tidal Wave is also extending its popular Founders Club offer through the Grand Opening celebration (October 28-November 8) - available on the top 3 wash plans, new members pay just $10 for their first month, then receive $10 off each month for the following 12 months, for 13 months of savings. New Tidal Wave members gain access to the entire 339-location networkspanning 30 states, offering unmatched convenience for customers on the go.

Tidal Wave is proud to invest in the communities it calls home, having donated more than $8.5 million to charitable organizations nationwide. In celebration of the Merritt Island grand opening, the company will host Giveback Day on Wednesday, November 4, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., donating $1 for every free wash and $5 for every new Tidal Wave Clean Club membership to The Children's Hunger Project. Donations will support The Children's Hunger Project's mission to provide weekend food packages to elementary school children in need across Brevard County - ensuring kids have access to nourishing food when school meals are unavailable. What started with one school and 27 children has grown to serve nearly 5,000 children across 60 schools, addressing a critical gap in a county where 70% of public elementary school students qualify for free or reduced meals.

"Opening our 33rd location in Florida in Merritt Island is an exciting step for Tidal Wave, and we're excited to bring our premium car wash experience to the heart of the Space Coast. We're also proud to support The Children's Hunger Project through our Giveback Day and help children across Brevard County get the nourishing food they need. We look forward to serving this community and becoming a trusted part of it," said Tidal Wave Auto Spa CEO and Founder, Scott Blackstock.

Tidal Wave proudly serves customers at 339 conveyor car wash locations across the United States, including 33 in Florida, with additional Sunshine State openings planned this year in Wimauma.

MOSES LAKE, Wash., Oct. 30, 2026

The article outlines how often patients should schedule cleanings to support gum health and long-term oral health maintenance.

MOSES LAKE, Wash., Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How often should you get dental cleanings to maintain a healthy smile? The answer is explored in a HelloNation article featuring insights from Dental Expert Dr. Calvin Despain of Skyview Dental in Moses Lake, Washington.

The HelloNation article explains that dental cleaning frequency plays a central role in maintaining oral health. For many adults, visiting the dentist every six months is considered standard. This timing allows for consistent plaque and tartar removal before buildup can lead to more serious concerns. The article emphasizes that even with strong brushing and flossing habits, plaque can accumulate daily and eventually harden into tartar that requires professional dental cleanings.

According to the article, professional dental cleanings are designed to reach areas that routine home care may miss. These visits help reduce harmful bacteria and support long-term gum health. Dental Expert Dr. Calvin Despain is featured in the article, which highlights how regular Moses Lake dental cleaning appointments can make future visits easier and more comfortable by limiting buildup between appointments.

The article notes that while a six-month schedule works well for many, dental cleaning frequency varies for everyone. Some patients may benefit from more frequent visits, such as every three to four months. This is often recommended for individuals with a history of gum disease, heavy buildup, or health conditions that affect oral health. The article explains that personalized care plans help ensure effective gum disease prevention and better long-term outcomes.

Gum health is a key focus throughout the article. It describes how plaque and tartar removal helps prevent inflammation that can lead to gingivitis. If untreated, gingivitis may progress into more advanced gum disease, potentially affecting the bone that supports teeth. Regular professional dental cleanings reduce these risks and support healthier gums.

The HelloNation article also connects oral health maintenance with overall health. It explains that gum health has been linked to broader conditions such as heart disease and complications related to diabetes. By maintaining consistent dental cleanings in Moses Lake, patients can reduce inflammation and support both oral and general health.

Another important benefit discussed is early detection. The article explains how routine visits enable dental professionals to identify issues such as cavities and gum recession at an early stage. Addressing these concerns early often leads to simpler treatments and helps patients avoid more complex procedures later. Dental Expert Dr. Calvin Despain is included in the article as a source of insight on how consistent monitoring supports effective gum disease prevention.

The article further explains that maintaining a steady dental cleaning frequency improves patient comfort over time. With less plaque and tartar buildup, appointments tend to be quicker and more predictable. This consistency encourages patients to stay on track with their oral health maintenance routines and reinforces the importance of regular care.

For residents seeking guidance, the article emphasizes that the right schedule depends on individual needs. Factors such as medical history, lifestyle habits, and current gum condition all play a role. A personalized approach ensures that professional dental cleanings remain effective and aligned with each patient's oral health goals.
